content: Welcome. First homework: send me the diagram of one system you've built that you're proudest of. Don't redraw it; send me what you actually had at the time.
Attaching the message queue diagram. The 'persistence' label is doing a lot of work that the system isn't actually doing. Embarrassing in retrospect.
That self-edit is the lesson. Bring the embarrassment to every review — it's the diagnostic.
For Thursday: write the 10x version of the queue. Don't redesign. Write the change list and the trade-offs.
Did the change list. Six items. The hard one is item three — the back-pressure strategy depends on the consumer model and I hadn't picked one.
Pick one tonight. We'll talk through the trade-off in our call.
Mock interview prep — I'm freezing on the 'estimate' question. Can we do one in our next session?
Sure. I'll throw three at you and you'll do them out loud. We'll record.
Welcome. First week's homework isn't code. Write me a single paragraph: what would your week look like if you were happy in five years. No filter.
Done. Wrote it. The week has more outdoor than computer in it. Honestly didn't expect that.
Interesting. Save it. We'll come back to it in month three when you're forced to choose.
For Friday: paper-prototype the first ten seconds of a hiking game. Just paper. Don't open Unity.
Paper sketches done. Found the first-ten-seconds problem is harder than the rest. Now I get the 'one paragraph' lesson better.
Quick check-in. How's the hiking-trail Flutter app coming this week?
Slower than I want. The GPS noise is real. But I made the architecture clearer; next push is the filter.
Read your CV. Before you write anything new: send me the question you genuinely care about. One sentence, no qualifiers.
How can NLP work as well in Turkish (low-resource morphologically rich language) as it does in English? Without industrial-scale data.
Good. Now write the research statement around that sentence. Three drafts before our call.
Three drafts in. The third is the least bad. Sending it.
Read it. The middle three paragraphs are good. The opening is a description, not an argument. The conclusion lists too many techniques. Concrete edits in line comments.
Rewrote the opening. The argument is now there, but I worry it's too confident. Senior researchers don't sound this sure of themselves.
Confidence is correct in a statement. Hedging belongs in papers, not in applications. Keep the new opening.
Welcome. First week: stop introducing yourself as 'not CS.' You're a person who reads documentation carefully. That's the actual job.
Noted. Hard habit to break but I'll try.
Try is fine. Easier with a small project to anchor to. We'll set one up Friday.
Docker multi-stage build finally clicked. 1.2GB → 180MB image. I keep posting these wins because the relief is real.
Good. Now we make it observable. Add metrics. The deploy is the start; operating is the job.
Scheduled the SAA exam for August. Mock test today: 68%. Need 72%. Two weeks on VPC and IAM.
Two focused weeks gets you there. Lab through the VPC peering scenarios. Stop reading; start breaking things.
Welcome. First month is a reading month. No CTFs. Twenty audit reports from established firms, then we talk.
Twenty? I was thinking ten was a lot. Will do.
Twenty. The pattern emerges around fifteen. Skip none.
Done with the twenty. The pattern: 70% of findings are configuration. The 'novel exploit' is the exception.
Now you're a different reader. We can talk OSCP, but with proper foundations. Schedule the exam for month four, not month two.
Wrote my first formal bug report this week. The disclosure timeline was painful to plan. Realized: report writing is its own discipline.
It is. Half the senior security work is writing. Save your drafts; we'll review them together.

Welcome. We do six months. Two-week cycles. Odd weeks: I send you a real architecture decision from my team; you write your own version blind before you see ours. Even weeks: code review on your app. Sound right?
Sounds right. I'll start tonight.
First decision attached as a PDF — pagination strategy for a feed with ~10k items, multi-platform. Write your version before opening ours.
Wrote mine. Going with cursor-based pagination because the existing offset-based was 'fighting me' on infinite scroll. Reading yours now.
Your reasoning is solid. We landed in the same place. One thing we did that you didn't — added a snapshot-version fingerprint to the cursor for staleness invalidation. Annotated PDF coming.
Did the second decision exercise this week — caching strategy. My version was worse than yours. Annotations were brutal and useful.
Brutal-and-useful is the right combination. Don't lose the willingness to be annotated.
Code review went long this week — I think I want to refactor my state-management layer end-to-end before adding the next feature. Going to take a week.
Take the week. The refactor is the work. Send me the ADR before you start.
ADR for the refactor attached. Want feedback before I touch the code.
Read it. Two suggestions — added in line comments on the PDF. Otherwise, ship it.
Refactor complete. App feels lighter. Going to write up the lessons for the next meeting.
Looking forward to it. We'll start the leadership-readiness arc next month — different shape of work.
First thing: stop saying you're a teacher pivoting. You're a communicator who can read data. Try that for a week and report back.
Caught myself using the old framing twice already today. Trying.
Send me your cover letter for the role we discussed. Don't polish — send the version you'd actually send.
Attached. Three paragraphs. The middle one apologizes again. I see it now.
First interview tomorrow. Two minutes on positioning before the call?
Yes please. Calling at 11:30.
Offer in writing today. Junior content strategist at a B2B SaaS. I'm going to take it.
Wonderful. Take it. We'll close out with a wrap session next week — pick the lessons we both want to write down.
Welcome. Three months. Daily writing, no exceptions. We'll meet weekly. By month three you'll have a defensible answer about whether research is for you. Are you in?
I'm in. I'll start the journal tonight.
Three weeks of journal entries reviewed. The first two weeks read like a student. The last week reads like someone who notices her own thinking. That's the signal. Keep going.
Read three interpretability papers this week. The third one had a methodology I want to learn — would it be okay if we spent next week's session on that one specifically?
That's exactly what I was hoping you'd ask. Send the PDF.
I'm starting to suspect I want a longer engagement next — but not necessarily on a PhD track. Wanted to flag it before our debrief.
Honest of you to surface early. We'll spend the last month on the next-step decision, not on more methodology.
Welcome. Three months ends with a decision. Yes, no, or 'shelf for a year' are all acceptable. 'Still thinking' is not. Are you in?
I'm in. Terrifying but in.
Send me the list of 30 customers you can drive to in a weekend. Cold names. Not friends-of-friends.
List sent. Driving Sakarya–Düzce route this weekend with the notebook.
Six honest conversations is great. Now: write the obituary for the startup if it fails. Three pages. Send before our call.
Obituary attached. Reading it back made me realize the cofounder gap is the killing blow, not the market.
Big call. Real call. How are you feeling about the shelf decision?
Surprisingly OK. Relieved, even. Going to apply to a junior product role at one of the companies I interviewed for discovery.
Sounds right. Let's write the wrap document and close cleanly. You're not done with founder thinking; you're done with this iteration.
One month. Hard stop. Three exercises, three meetings, one decision. If you waver, I'll close the engagement early. Are you in?
In. Hard stop helps.
Customer discovery round one done. You hated it. Note that — it's data, not failure.
Hated the cold outreach, loved the conversations once I was in them. Mixed signal.
Obituary exercise: write three pages on why your startup would fail. Send before our last call.
Obituary done. The dominant failure mode is that I wouldn't enjoy the day-to-day operationally. Even if the idea is right, the temperament isn't.
That's a real answer. We close on Tuesday.
Aras — you keep commenting on the Vespa post. Are you actually shopping or just looking?
Half-actually. The Erzurum winter is brutal on a bike but the rest of the year is fine. I'm eyeing a used GTS but the import paperwork is intimidating.
Skip the import unless you find a 2019+ model in good shape locally. I bought mine from a Beşiktaş showroom — they handle paperwork. Cost ten percent more, saved a month of headaches.
Worth it. Sending you a listing tomorrow — want a sanity check on whether the price is fair.

Different question — you wrote that thing about 2am incidents and senior calmness. We're hitting the same in games production but the metric is the deadline, not the alarm. Lessons translate one-to-one in my experience.
They do. The skill is exactly the same: presence under public stress. The artifact is different. We should swap mentees for a session some time — give them both perspectives.
Half-serious offer? I have a mentee (İsmail) who's torn between mobile and games. He'd genuinely benefit from a one-off with you.
Fully serious. Send him my way for a single session. I'll do the same with Tolga at some point — he's interested in production at scale.
Saw your 'rename soft skills' post. Endorsed completely. We're trying to do this in EM circles too but the term has been baked into HR systems for two decades.
It's a soft battle. The renaming has to come from within the discipline. We're calling them 'craft skills' in our studio now. Slow adoption.
What's the in-meeting trigger for using 'craft' instead? Or is it just consistent practice?

Consistent practice. I correct myself out loud when I slip. Made it a rule that I don't use 'soft skills' in 1:1s with juniors. After three months, my direct team picked it up. Took six months for the rest of production to follow.
Trying the same in EM. Will report back at year-end. Also — completely separate — if you ever want a sounding board on engineering-management questions from a games-production lens, I'm here.
Same offer back. The discipline overlap is bigger than people realize.

Neslihan — your 'defensible AI' framing landed with me. We spend a lot of literature time arguing about explainability as the goal. You're right that for regulated contexts, defensibility is the actual deliverable. I want to teach this to our master's students.
Glad it resonated. The pedagogical gap between academic ML and regulated-industry practice is wider than people admit. If you ever want a guest seminar for your students, I'd be happy.
Yes — let's schedule it for autumn term. Topic: 'reading a model documentation pack critically.' Two hours, no slides — just a real pack and questions.
Perfect. I'll bring a sanitized real one from a recent committee review. The students will get more from one of those than ten textbook examples.
Also: I have a mentee (Mina, applying for ML PhDs) who's interested in responsible AI as a thesis topic. Would you be willing to give her 20 minutes to discuss it?
Of course. Send me her statement when she's ready; I'll come prepared.
